as_told: A university statistics department told its email administrator that it could not send email more than about 500 miles. The administrator tested it and found it was true. A software upgrade had set the connection timeout to almost zero, so the server gave up before a reply could come back from any host farther away than light could travel in about 3 milliseconds.
lesson: A user report that sounds impossible can be literally true, so test it and look for what changed in the system.
what_happened: Trey Harris posted the story to the sage-members mailing list on 24 November 2002. In a later FAQ he said it really happened to him while he ran the campus email system at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, some time between 1994 and 1997. He said he had no email, logs or notes from the time. He also said that he changed details for the story: the work took several hours, not minutes, and the 3-millisecond figure was not itself the timeout but an effective figure he worked out from ping times. The core claim, that a downgraded Sendmail with a Sendmail 8 configuration file stopped mail beyond a radius of a little more than 500 miles, he stood by.

lesson_verdict.why: I found no study or official record on how often user reports that sound impossible turn out to be true. The story is one case told by the person it happened to, and he says it is a humorous story, not a case study.

source.quote: I was writing a humorous story based on an actual occurence, not a case study

confidence_note: The only record is the teller's own account, written years later, with no logs, notes or other witnesses. 'True' here means that the teller, who is the person it happened to, says the core event happened; the technical details in the 2002 post are simplified by his own admission. No independent record confirms or rules out the event.
